notes.title: Thanks, Updates and Experimental Changes!
notes.content:
Hello everyone!

First off, huge thanks to all of you who’ve jumped into the Trainfort alpha and shared your feedback so far: it really means the world to the all team. Based on your enthusiasm, we decided to [b]keep the playtest open for now![/b]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45517724/9006c8a40d0a4347cf6bedccf395a5d1159a5a45.gif[/img]

With that decision comes also a [b]new update with a batch of improvements and fixes[/b], including:

[b][list]
[*] Battery packs now have an indicator
[*] Machines now have 2 buttons for packing
[*] Steam generator fuel consumption fixed
[*] Various power grid fixes
[*] Minor tweaks to machines
[*] Character now bound to Steam ID instead of nickname
[*] Teleport to spawn if you get stuck
[*] Resource container can now be packed
[*] Journal no longer spams new entry notifications
[*] Cartridge decoder now alerts if data was already extracted
[/list][/b]
[h3]But that’s not all…[/h3]

Based on feedback, we implemented [b]one experimental change[/b] we’d love your thoughts on. We noticed players were squatting a lot to pick up items, which could get tiring for some. So with the change now you can pick up things off the ground without crouching! You’ll still need to squat sometimes, just not as often 

Let us know what you think in the comment section below or on [b]Discord[/b] [b][url=https://discord.gg/zq8q5VUhh7]here[/url]! [/b]

Thanks again! [i]See you on the road![/i]

notes.title: Playtest Hotfix #1 is live!
notes.content:
- Fixed a bug that did not allow to craft the locomotive
- Fixed the screen on the Data Cards. Now it correctly shows the blueprint inside

Thank you for all the feedback! The team is hard at work preparing more fixes and improvements for the playtest. Stay tuned!

notes.title: Trainfort Devlog: Biomes & Exploration
notes.content:
[b]Hello everyone![/b]

Welcome to the second devlog about Trainfort! In this series, we’re sharing different parts of the game’s design, from systems to worldbuilding to the little details behind the scenes. Today we’ll talk about the biomes, what makes them special, and why the world is built to keep you moving.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45517724/3cd7e4ff50d507e7bd1a5c201613906370f1f2fa.gif[/img]

[h3][b]The Biomes of Trainfort[/b][/h3]
Right now, there are two main zones in the world of Trainfort. The first is the “regular” zone, which includes forests, fields, deserts, and mountains. These are relatively safe (at least during the day) and give each area a different feel as you travel. The second is the “infested” zone: same biomes, but much more hostile. Toxic air, dangerous creatures, and a time limit on how long you can survive without protection.

The game uses "areas" as modifiers for biomes. So a forest might be part of the regular zone or the infested one, depending on where you are. Infested zones come with dead trees, aggressive monsters, toxic gas, and special resources or structures that can’t be found anywhere else. You’ll need proper gear just to stay alive there, but they’re also home to unique technologies and progression materials.

In the future, we’d love to add more area types, like frozen zones or volcanic regions. These could come with their own hazards, like strong winds or lava geysers, and force players to change their approach completely.

Each biome also plays differently depending on terrain and visibility. For example, forests can give you cover but make it harder to spot threats, while open fields are great for movement but leave you exposed.

[h3][b]The Real Reward in Exploring[/b][/h3]
You won’t find any achievement pop-ups for visiting a new biome. That’s intentional! Instead, we wanted the world itself to be the reason to explore. Certain areas are rich in lootable structures, and some are even hidden underground. The infested zones in particular are packed with tough enemies and high-value rewards.

So if you’re wondering whether it’s worth leaving your starting area, the answer is… YES, you have to move!

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45517724/b3e7112ad67333572e5855dc71affae490f6c2d8.gif[/img]

[h3][b]How Exploration Works[/b][/h3]
One key detail: resources don’t respawn. This means that staying in one place forever won’t work. The world is designed in clusters, where interesting locations spawn together, but each group is far apart. You could try to bring everything back to your first base… but packing it all up and moving is usually much easier. And would you look at that: as luck would have it, packing is really the focus of our game ;) (if you haven’t checked our first devlog about Packing in Trainfort yet, pack your stuff and go read it here)

[h3][b]Nomads at Heart[/b][/h3]
We’re still tuning the systems, but everything, from packing, to biome placement, to resource distribution, is designed to support a nomadic playstyle. We really want players to keep moving, discovering new zones, and adapting their setup as they go.

The mobile base idea came from older RTS games like Red Alert 2, where you had construction vehicles that could deploy into buildings. Over time, we turned that concept into something that works for survival gameplay.

The current system is a balance between functionality and weirdness. The animation is simple, but under the hood, it’s the same system we use to load the whole world, save inventory items, and even remember the contents of shrinkable machines.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45517724/b4df6dc07ef01915821dc692146a653e927c0e4c.gif[/img]

[h3][b]Tick-Tock, time is passing![/b][/h3]
The day/night cycle is more than just a visual change. In the regular zone, nighttime means spores start spawning monsters, making travel much more dangerous. We’re planning to make each area behave differently depending on the time of day, with new threats, new opportunities, and another reason to stay alert while you explore.

We’re also not following the usual survival blueprints. Games like Space Engineers let you build complex structures, but they don’t move or pack away. We wanted to refresh the formula by giving players more control, more movement, and more reasons to leave their comfort zone.

That’s all for today! We’ll be back soon with another devlog. Until then, we hope you’re enjoying the alpha, and don’t forget to share your thoughts with us here, on itch.io or on Discord. See you!

notes.title: Trainfort Devlog: Packing & Shrinking
notes.content:
[b]Hello everyone![/b]

Welcome to the first [b]devlog[/b] about [b]Trainfort[/b]! In this series we will cover many aspects of the game, like the controls, storing methods, levels and dungeons. Today we are going to tell you more about the Packing system in game.

One of the core mechanics in the game is the ability to [b]pack up your base, vehicles, and equipment, turning them into compact, portable items that can be carried around[/b]. This system was designed to let players operate a mobile base, allowing players to embrace a truly nomadic lifestyle.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45517724/9006c8a40d0a4347cf6bedccf395a5d1159a5a45.gif[/img]

[h2][b]How It Works[/b][/h2]
Our goal was to make packing feel like holding a detailed miniature version of your gear. Most of the large craftable objects can be packed. Vehicles, base foundations, workbenches. However, already packed items can’t be packed again (so no infinite nesting of objects).

For you as a player, this means complete freedom: you can set up a base, make it precisely how you and your group want it, then shrink it all down and bring it along when you move to a new location.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45517724/581e1944a6d226df5612f5c0339e539c71e41b65.gif[/img]

[h2][b]Challenges & Early Versions[/b][/h2]
The packing system has been in place since [b]early development[/b], but balancing it was another story. At one point, players could pack a locomotive inside a base foundation, pack that foundation into a backpack, then pack the backpack into another backpack… endlessly. While technically impressive, it quickly became clear that some limits were needed hahaha!

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45517724/d6286f8a7272c1f6e62a9827c985141356093b2f.png[/img]

Another major challenge was saving packed objects properly. The same system that handles packing also loads the entire world around the player and keeps track of items in backpacks or stored inside shrinkable machines. Getting everything to work together without breaking the game took time.

Early on, we experimented with different effects to make the shrinking process look satisfying. The goal was to strike a balance between clear visual feedback and technical feasibility, making sure players always understood what was happening without overcomplicating animations.

We always wanted deployment to look cool, and at some point there was a reference to how buildings "unfold" in [b]C&C games[/b]. But, given how many different in-game objects use that system, we had to go with something simpler but universal.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45517724/618bf0be8614427cb5d12ef711631da5526df3a4.gif[/img]


[h2][b]Players’ Experimentation and the Future of Packing[/b][/h2]
So far, players have already come up with some unexpected uses for the system. One group built a [b]zoo maze for monsters[/b] to test their AI, using packed objects as part of the experiment. Seeing how the community pushes the mechanics in ways we never anticipated is one of the most exciting parts of development.

Another aspect that might not be final is that [b]packing and unpacking now happen instantly[/b]. You press a button, and in [b]3 seconds[/b], the base is deployed. In the future, we might introduce additional limitations, like time or resources needed to deploy, especially for bigger bases with many items.

We [b]love[/b] the system, but there’s always room to refine it. We’re still thinking about ways to improve how it interacts with the rest of the game, making sure it stays balanced and engaging as Trainfort evolves.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45517724/1838cd6f5854294bf62349cf202c5264b9ef8353.gif[/img]

That’s all for today, hope you are enjoying the game, be sure to let us know what you think here, on itch.io or on our Discord. See you!
